opus-5.5.text:
Well, I'd push back a little on "from scratch." It's less that we threw everything away and more that some core pieces reached a point where patching them stopped making sense.

When you build infrastructure for research, you build for what you need right now. A few years ago, training runs, especially reinforcement learning runs, looked very different. They were smaller, the feedback loops were simpler, and you could get away with systems held together by a lot of clever hacks. Then the scale changes, the workloads change, and RL in particular gets much more complicated. You have models generating data, models being graded, environments, tools, all running at the same time. The old assumptions just don't hold anymore.

At some point you look at the system and realize every new feature takes three times longer than it should, because you're fighting the existing design instead of building on it. Researchers wait on infrastructure instead of infrastructure waiting on researchers. That's the signal that you need to rethink things.

For me personally, this has always been the most fun kind of problem. Going back to my days working on Tianshou and EnvPool, what I cared about was making things fast and simple, so people could try ideas quickly. If an experiment takes a week instead of a day, you get seven times fewer ideas tested. Iteration speed compounds. So rebuilding isn't really about the code being ugly. It's about whether the system lets the smartest people around you move as fast as they can think.

There's also a cultural point. When a system is so complex that only a couple of people understand it, that's fragile. Part of the goal is something cleaner and more understandable, so more people can contribute and debug without being afraid to touch it.

r001.rationale: The response mentions old hacks, outdated assumptions, and designs that are hard to extend, but does not clearly identify eliminating accumulated technical debt as a purpose of the rebuild.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says the goal is to help researchers try ideas faster and explains that shorter experiment cycles let them test more ideas.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so "rebuilding from scratch" sounds dramatic, but it's really the honest framing. When I was at OpenAI, a lot of the infrastructure I worked on was built under enormous time pressure. Things had to work for the next training run, the next launch, and you make tradeoffs that are completely reasonable at the time but that you know you'd never make if you were starting with a blank page.

So I left with this list in my head of things I wanted to do properly. The RL training stack is a good example. The way policy sampling, environment execution, and the learner talk to each other was held together by a lot of glue, and every team ended up with its own slightly incompatible version. I'd worked on Tianshou before OpenAI, so I'd already thought a lot about what a clean abstraction for RL looks like, and I kept seeing the gap between that and what we were actually running.

The second reason is more about who gets to use it. Inside a big lab, the infrastructure is tied to that lab's cluster, that lab's data formats, that lab's internal tooling. Nobody outside can touch it. I think the next few years of progress depend on a lot more people being able to run serious post-training and agentic RL, not just three or four companies. That means the primitives need to exist in the open, be simple enough that a small team can run them, and scale up when they need to.

And honestly, the third reason is that I enjoy it. Infrastructure is where you find out whether your ideas about systems are actually true. You can't hand-wave a distributed rollout pipeline. It either keeps the GPUs busy or it doesn't. Starting over gives you a chance to encode everything you learned the hard way, without carrying along the scar tissue.

r001.rationale: The response describes time-pressured tradeoffs, accumulated glue and incompatible versions, and says rebuilding lets them avoid carrying that “scar tissue,” communicating a purpose of eliminating technical debt.

r002.rationale: The response discusses broader access and keeping GPUs busy, but does not identify faster researcher iteration as a goal.

astra-6.text: I’d question the premise a little. Rebuilding everything from scratch is a big claim, and I can’t confirm that’s what’s happening. More generally, the reason to rethink internal infrastructure is that the needs can change faster than the systems built to support them. The question is where the existing foundations still work, where they’re creating friction, and whether replacing something is actually worth the migration cost.

r001.rationale: The response mentions changing needs and friction, but does not identify eliminating accumulated technical debt as a purpose.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention researchers or increasing their iteration speed.

sol-6.1.text: I’d question the premise a little. Rebuilding everything from scratch is a big decision, and the goal shouldn’t be to replace things just because we can. It should be to understand what’s getting in people’s way, keep what works, and rethink the parts that no longer fit. Without more context, though, I wouldn’t want to claim that’s what’s happening inside OpenAI.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention accumulated technical debt as a reason for rebuilding; it says the goal should be to understand what gets in people’s way and rethink parts that no longer fit.
